variables_mentioned: how often respondents felt happy and in a good mood (2017)
six items on ability to carry out everyday activities
contact with grandchildren, extended family, friends and acquaintances

registers.name_in_paper: administrative register data (overview in Section B of the online supplementary materials)
registers.role: controls (education, income, cardiovascular diseases, cancer, labor market status, cohabitation) and linkage; the individual registers are named only in the online supplementary materials
variables_mentioned: disposable individualized income coded into deciles
indicator variables for being diagnosed with cardiovascular diseases and cancer

linkages: DLSA survey respondents merged with individual-level Danish National Prescription Registry records on redeemed antidepressant prescriptions from 1995

sample.universe: Participants in the Danish Longitudinal Study of Aging, which started in 1997 as a prospective cohort study of individuals aged 52 to 77, observed in the 2012 and 2017 waves (birth cohorts 1920-1960)
sample.unit_of_observation: person-year (data restructured into person-year format, one record for each person-year combination, restricted to years at risk)
selection_rules: Use only the 2012 and 2017 DLSA waves, because questions about volunteering were omitted in 2002 and 2007
Focus on the 2012-2018 period, giving up to seven observations per respondent
Exclude respondents who took antidepressants throughout the entire investigation period
Exclude respondents with missing data (these two exclusions together account for approximately five percent of the initial sample)
Keep only years in which respondents were at risk of starting a spell of antidepressant use, i.e. when they were not yet using antidepressants in the preceding year
Allow people who first start and then stop using antidepressants to re-enter the risk set, so multiple at-risk spells are observed for some individuals
sample.period: 2012-2018 (antidepressant use measured in the register from 1995; histories used for 1995-2003 and 2004-2011)

construction_notes: DLSA-based variables are interpolated for the years not covered by the survey: respondents' characteristics (e.g. volunteering status) for non-DLSA years are set equal to their characteristics in the closest DLSA year, which retroactively assigns 2015 and 2016 values from the 2017 wave

Volunteering intensity is bracketed as no volunteering, less than 50 h per year, 50-99 h per year, and 100 or more hours per year; the paper notes there is no theoretical basis for these specific brackets
The four organization-type indicators (religious, sports, social service, other) are separate indicator variables that are not mutually exclusive, so some people volunteer for multiple organizations

Antidepressants are defined as all ATC codes starting with N06A; drugs used during hospital admissions, by institutionalized individuals, or supplied directly by hospitals or treatment centres are not in the DNPR
Functional impairments are the average of six items capturing respondents' ability to carry out everyday activities (e.g. washing, climbing stairs), scaled 0-2

Mental health problems is a time-varying dummy built from the 2012 question on how often respondents felt depressed and the 2017 question on how often they felt happy and in a good mood; its incidence is 2 percent in both 2012 and 2017, and only 0.3 percent of respondents are classified as having problems in both years
Education is highest completed education by 2012 (primary, vocational, further); income is disposable individualized income coded into deciles (1-10)

Histories of antidepressant use are indicator variables for any use in 2004-2011 (relatively recent) and 1995-2003 (more historical), going back as far as 17 years before volunteering is first measured

Table 1's summary statistics for all time-varying variables pertain to the last year before censoring; for antidepressant use between 2012 and 2018 it shows the proportion of people who at any point during this window use antidepressants (0.09)

Labor market status, cohabitation status, everyday physical activity, sports participation, contacts with family and friends, and religious service attendance are only included in the supplementary analyses

claims.statement: Doing any volunteering in the past year reduces the odds of starting antidepressant use in a given year among older Danish adults, in a model that controls only for time at risk.

register_source.value: Danish Longitudinal Study of Aging (DLSA), 2012 and 2017 waves -- survey data, not a Danish administrative register

definition.value: Binary variable for doing any volunteering during the past year, constructed from DLSA items asking respondents whether they had volunteered in 14 different areas; measured in the 2012 and 2017 waves and interpolated to the non-DLSA years by setting characteristics equal to those in the closest DLSA year.

timing.value: Time-varying regressor vol_it; measured in the 2012 and 2017 DLSA waves and carried to the remaining years of 2012-2018 from the closest DLSA year

register_source.value: Danish National Prescription Registry (DNPR): all Anatomical Therapeutical Chemical (ATC) codes starting with N06A

definition.value: The event of starting antidepressant use during the 2012-2018 window: coded zero in years where an individual is not using antidepressants and one in years where they start using antidepressants. Antidepressants are all ATC codes starting with N06A redeemed at Danish community pharmacies (recorded in the DNPR since 1995). Only person-years in which the respondent was 'at risk' (not using antidepressants in the preceding year) enter the risk set; people who stop using antidepressants may re-enter the risk set.

timing.value: Annually over 2012-2018 (up to seven person-years per respondent), measured as the conditional probability of starting a spell of antidepressant use in a given year at risk

units.value: odds ratio: multiplicative change in the odds of starting antidepressant use in a given year, relative to the reference category

magnitude.interpretation: volunteers have 32 percent lower odds of starting antidepressant use than non-volunteers

subgroups_defined: Volunteering intensity: no volunteering, 1-49 h, 50-99 h, 100 h or more per year
Type of voluntary organization: sports-oriented, social service, religious-oriented, other
Individuals aged 65 and over (supplementary Section A)
population.selection: DLSA survey respondents in the 2012 and 2017 waves (cross-sectional response rates 75 and 68 percent; 2012-2017 retention 78 percent), excluding respondents who used antidepressants throughout the entire investigation period and those with missing data (together about five percent of the initial sample), and retaining only person-years in which the respondent was at risk of starting a spell of antidepressant use

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: the paper compares volunteers with non-volunteers (and intensities/organization types with non-volunteering) in observational DLSA data, adjusting for a rich set of register- and survey-based confounders -- most importantly 17 years of prior antidepressant-use history (1995-2003 and 2004-2011) -- plus birth-cohort and time-at-risk fixed effects and an individual-specific random effect

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional ignorability: conditional on the included controls, the cohort and time-at-risk fixed effects and the individual random effect, volunteering is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of starting antidepressant use (no remaining common-cause confounding).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the control set by the known differences between volunteers and non-volunteers and states that the analyses may be subject to common-cause confounding if these factors are not sufficiently controlled for; it reports supplementary analyses with an expanded control set (Section F) and with individual fixed effects (Section D).

implies_edges.from: control variables (sex, birth cohort, education, income decile, cardiovascular diseases, cancer, functional impairments)

key_assumptions.assumption: The main-analysis control variables are not themselves influenced by volunteering, so conditioning on them does not block part of the effect of interest (no overcontrol bias from mediators).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated directly in the description of the control variables; a broader control set that may carry overcontrol risk is relegated to supplementary analyses (Section F).

key_assumptions.assumption: Controlling for antidepressant use in 1995-2003 and 2004-2011 captures the reverse-causal channel from medical history to volunteering, i.e. antidepressant/depression history before 1995 has no further independent effect on volunteering in 2012-2017.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper controls for histories of antidepressant use going back as far as 17 years before volunteering is first measured, and argues it is crucial to do so as far back as possible; the DNPR starts in 1995, so no earlier history is observed.

key_assumptions.assumption: The individual-specific random effect u_i is uncorrelated with the model's error term (and with the covariates), so that it absorbs time-constant unobserved heterogeneity rather than biasing the volunteering coefficient.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated when the random effect is introduced; the paper additionally runs individual fixed-effects regressions on the 2012 and 2017 waves (Section D), which give consistent but statistically insignificant coefficients.

key_assumptions.assumption: Volunteering (and the other DLSA variables) in the years not covered by the survey equals the value observed in the closest DLSA year, so the interpolated person-years carry the correct treatment status.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The interpolation rule is stated explicitly; robustness analyses that instead project the affected variables forward are reported in Section C, and analyses restricted to the DLSA years in Section D.

key_assumptions.assumption: Redeemed prescriptions in the DNPR measure antidepressant use: people who redeem a prescription use the drug, and the transactions missing from the DNPR (hospital admissions, institutionalized individuals, drugs supplied directly by hospitals or treatment centres) do not distort the onset measure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper lists the two caveats and the three excluded transaction types, and notes that patients who continue using antidepressants after dismissal from these institutions will show up in the DNPR.

key_assumptions.assumption: Selection into the analytic sample -- DLSA survey response and retention, exclusion of respondents using antidepressants throughout the whole period or with missing data, and the restriction to person-years at risk -- does not bias the estimated effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reports response rates of 75 and 68 percent and a retention rate of 78 percent and argues these high rates matter because nonresponse is likely related to both volunteering and mental health; it states that the exclusions account for about five percent of the initial sample.

threats_discussed: Self-selection into volunteering: volunteers have higher socioeconomic status, more extensive social networks and better physical and mental health
Reverse causation: past antidepressant use and a history of depression may reduce the propensity to volunteer
Lagged effects of mental health histories before the study baseline, which controlling for baseline symptoms alone would not address
Overcontrol bias from conditioning on variables that are themselves influenced by volunteering (mediators)
Time-constant unobserved heterogeneity, e.g. genetic factors, in the baseline risk of antidepressant use
Retroactively assigning 2015 and 2016 values from the 2017 wave risks introducing reverse causality
Survey nonresponse is likely related to both volunteering and mental health

Antidepressant transactions not captured by the DNPR (hospital admissions, institutionalized individuals, drugs supplied directly by hospitals or treatment centres), and prescriptions redeemed but not used
robustness_checks: Projecting the DLSA-based variables forward for all years not covered by the DLSA instead of using the closest wave (Section C)
Analyses restricted to the DLSA years with individual fixed effects and lagged dependent variable models (Section D)
Narrower volunteering-intensity brackets (Section E)
An expanded set of control variables including labor market status, cohabitation, physical activity, social contacts and religious service attendance (Section F)
Not allowing people to re-enter the risk set after a first period of antidepressant use (Section G)
Interaction terms between volunteering and mental health problems (Section H)
Excluding individuals under 65 (Section A)
unresolved_confounders: Time-constant unobserved variables correlated with the model's error term: the random effect only absorbs them insofar as they are uncorrelated with it, and the individual fixed-effects models that would rule them out more fully are no longer statistically significant

fixed_effects: time at risk (time fixed effects; the baseline logit hazard is modelled as a step function with time fixed effects, where time signifies the number of years at risk)

source_table.value: Table 2, Model 1

adjustment_set.label: time at risk (time fixed effects / time dummies)

mediators_claimed: Prevention or alleviation of depressive symptoms (mental health problems), adjusted for in Model 4 of Table 2 and Models 2 and 4 of Table 3
Increased availability of social support through a larger and more diverse social network
A strengthened sense of purpose, meaning and 'mattering', and the self-esteem and self-efficacy that follow from it
Better access to non-medical treatments such as counseling, which may postpone or replace antidepressant treatment

heterogeneity.finding: Moderate-intensity volunteering (50-99 h) shows the largest reduction in the odds of onset (OR 0.57 in Model 1 and 0.58 in Model 2 of Table 3), while 1-49 h and 100 h or more are closer to one and statistically insignificant

No clear evidence that the effect depends on the type of organization volunteered for; the estimated odds ratios for sports, social service, religious and other organizations do not show a clear pattern and their confidence intervals overlap

population.selection: DLSA survey respondents in the 2012 and 2017 waves (cross-sectional response rates 75 and 68 percent; 2012-2017 retention 78 percent), excluding respondents who used antidepressants throughout the entire investigation period and those with missing data (together about five percent of the initial sample), and retaining only person-years in which the respondent was at risk of starting a spell of antidepressant use

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: the paper compares volunteers with non-volunteers (and intensities/organization types with non-volunteering) in observational DLSA data, adjusting for a rich set of register- and survey-based confounders -- most importantly 17 years of prior antidepressant-use history (1995-2003 and 2004-2011) -- plus birth-cohort and time-at-risk fixed effects and an individual-specific random effect

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional ignorability: conditional on the included controls, the cohort and time-at-risk fixed effects and the individual random effect, volunteering is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of starting antidepressant use (no remaining common-cause confounding).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the control set by the known differences between volunteers and non-volunteers and states that the analyses may be subject to common-cause confounding if these factors are not sufficiently controlled for; it reports supplementary analyses with an expanded control set (Section F) and with individual fixed effects (Section D).

implies_edges.from: control variables (sex, birth cohort, education, income decile, cardiovascular diseases, cancer, functional impairments)

key_assumptions.assumption: The main-analysis control variables are not themselves influenced by volunteering, so conditioning on them does not block part of the effect of interest (no overcontrol bias from mediators).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated directly in the description of the control variables; a broader control set that may carry overcontrol risk is relegated to supplementary analyses (Section F).

key_assumptions.assumption: Controlling for antidepressant use in 1995-2003 and 2004-2011 captures the reverse-causal channel from medical history to volunteering, i.e. antidepressant/depression history before 1995 has no further independent effect on volunteering in 2012-2017.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper controls for histories of antidepressant use going back as far as 17 years before volunteering is first measured, and argues it is crucial to do so as far back as possible; the DNPR starts in 1995, so no earlier history is observed.

key_assumptions.assumption: The individual-specific random effect u_i is uncorrelated with the model's error term (and with the covariates), so that it absorbs time-constant unobserved heterogeneity rather than biasing the volunteering coefficient.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated when the random effect is introduced; the paper additionally runs individual fixed-effects regressions on the 2012 and 2017 waves (Section D), which give consistent but statistically insignificant coefficients.

key_assumptions.assumption: Volunteering (and the other DLSA variables) in the years not covered by the survey equals the value observed in the closest DLSA year, so the interpolated person-years carry the correct treatment status.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The interpolation rule is stated explicitly; robustness analyses that instead project the affected variables forward are reported in Section C, and analyses restricted to the DLSA years in Section D.

key_assumptions.assumption: Redeemed prescriptions in the DNPR measure antidepressant use: people who redeem a prescription use the drug, and the transactions missing from the DNPR (hospital admissions, institutionalized individuals, drugs supplied directly by hospitals or treatment centres) do not distort the onset measure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper lists the two caveats and the three excluded transaction types, and notes that patients who continue using antidepressants after dismissal from these institutions will show up in the DNPR.

key_assumptions.assumption: Selection into the analytic sample -- DLSA survey response and retention, exclusion of respondents using antidepressants throughout the whole period or with missing data, and the restriction to person-years at risk -- does not bias the estimated effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reports response rates of 75 and 68 percent and a retention rate of 78 percent and argues these high rates matter because nonresponse is likely related to both volunteering and mental health; it states that the exclusions account for about five percent of the initial sample.

implies_edges.from: at risk of starting antidepressant use (risk-set membership) and DLSA survey participation

key_assumptions.assumption: Mental health problems are a mediator rather than a confounder of the volunteering-antidepressant use relationship, so the coefficient with mental health adjusted identifies the effect operating over and above mental health.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The introduction states that mental health is adjusted for in several analyses in order to assess whether volunteering affects antidepressant use only through the likelihood of poor mental health or also through other mechanisms.

threats_discussed: Self-selection into volunteering: volunteers have higher socioeconomic status, more extensive social networks and better physical and mental health
Reverse causation: past antidepressant use and a history of depression may reduce the propensity to volunteer
Lagged effects of mental health histories before the study baseline, which controlling for baseline symptoms alone would not address
Overcontrol bias from conditioning on variables that are themselves influenced by volunteering (mediators)
Time-constant unobserved heterogeneity, e.g. genetic factors, in the baseline risk of antidepressant use
Retroactively assigning 2015 and 2016 values from the 2017 wave risks introducing reverse causality
Survey nonresponse is likely related to both volunteering and mental health

Antidepressant transactions not captured by the DNPR (hospital admissions, institutionalized individuals, drugs supplied directly by hospitals or treatment centres), and prescriptions redeemed but not used
robustness_checks: Projecting the DLSA-based variables forward for all years not covered by the DLSA instead of using the closest wave (Section C)
Analyses restricted to the DLSA years with individual fixed effects and lagged dependent variable models (Section D)
Narrower volunteering-intensity brackets (Section E)
An expanded set of control variables including labor market status, cohabitation, physical activity, social contacts and religious service attendance (Section F)
Not allowing people to re-enter the risk set after a first period of antidepressant use (Section G)
Interaction terms between volunteering and mental health problems (Section H)
Excluding individuals under 65 (Section A)
unresolved_confounders: Time-constant unobserved variables correlated with the model's error term: the random effect only absorbs them insofar as they are uncorrelated with it, and the individual fixed-effects models that would rule them out more fully are no longer statistically significant
Pre-observation volunteering histories: individuals who appear to begin volunteering during the observation window might merely be resuming a previous pattern of volunteering
The mechanisms behind the effect could not be directly confronted in the empirical analysis
Whether the effect manifests itself immediately after people start volunteering or only after a sustained period of involvement cannot be verified
